title: Davenant: conscience-wasting falls are singularly mortal; defects in good works are not
source_text: XXIX. Simili modo videtur explicare distinctionem peccati in mortale & veniale, Joannes Davenantius Episcopus Sarisburiensis. Nam mortalia vocat ratione singulari peccata illa graviora quae conscientiam vastant, & novo mortis aeternae reatu constringunt fideles ipsos qui in ea labuntur, eosque, quamdiu ab iis non resurgunt, ineptos reddunt qui in regnum coelorum ingrediantur. Ad quod genus peccatorum non pertinere docet defectus qui bonis ipsorum operibus adhaerent atque intermixti sunt, licet peccati rationem habeant, & juxta summum legis rigorem mortem mereantur. Unde concludit ejusmodi defectus, peccata mortalia appropriate dici non debere. Ut apud ipsum videre est, De Justitia actuali, cap. 35.
pass_a_gloss: In a like way John Davenant, Bishop of Salisbury, seems to explain the distinction of sin into mortal and venial. For by a singular reason he calls mortal those graver sins which waste the conscience and bind the very faithful who fall into them with a new guilt of eternal death, and render them, so long as they do not rise from them, unfit to enter the kingdom of heaven. To which kind of sins he teaches that the defects which cling to and are mixed with their good works do not belong, although they have the nature of sin and according to the utmost rigor of the law merit death. Whence he concludes that defects of that kind ought not to be called mortal sins appropriately. As may be seen in him, On actual righteousness, chapter 35.
pass_b_english: Davenant: singularly mortal are conscience-wasting falls that newly bind believers under death-guilt.
Flaws mixed into good works, though truly sinful by law’s rigor, are not appropriately called mortal.

choices.why: Flaws adhering to good works, not capital falls.
